note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A company plans to buy an old factory in Spanish Town. Why should it pay for an evaluation of the electrical installation first?
options: To learn its condition, capacity and upgrade costs before buying
To get the old installation approved without any testing being done
To find a reason to lower the price of the land and nothing more
To let the seller's electrician carry on with the maintenance work

questions.stem: What should the client's brief for an evaluation make clear before the work starts?
options: The colour scheme planned for all of the new shops in the plaza
The names of every tenant's staff and the hours they work
The purpose, the areas covered and the questions to answer
The rent that each tenant pays every month

questions.stem: A client must decide whether to accept a new installation from a contractor. Against what should it be evaluated?
options: The contractor's own opinion of how good the work is
The design, the specification and the contract
How the installation in the building next door was done
The cheapest way that the work could have been done

questions.stem: During an evaluation, the client cannot find any drawings or test records. What is the best step?
options: Pass the installation, since nothing shows that it has failed
Stop the evaluation until the first contractor can be traced and asked
Assume every cable is the size printed on its breaker
Note the gap, trace and record key circuits, and allow more time

questions.stem: A 200 A main switch has a logged maximum demand of 170 A. What percentage of its rating is being used?
Why is a power logger usually left on a main board for at least a week during an evaluation?
options: It charges up the board's backup batteries over the week
It keeps the meter reading lower for that month
It records the real peaks and patterns over normal days
It removes the need to inspect the boards at all

questions.stem: A logger shows line 1 at 52 A and line 2 at 30 A on a 110/220 V board with mostly resistive 110 V loads. What does this show?
options: The board is well balanced and needs no action
The lines are out of balance; about 22 A flows in the neutral
The power company's meter is faulty and has to be changed at once
All of the 220 V loads must be moved over to 110 V

questions.stem: Logged voltage at the far end of a 110 V outlet circuit falls to 98 V when a photocopier runs. What should the evaluator do?
options: Ignore it, because 98 V is close enough to 110 V
Change the outlet for one with a higher current rating on it
Fit a bigger breaker so that the voltage comes back up to 110 V
Compare it with the specification; check volt drop and joints

questions.stem: In a workshop, the lights dim each time a large compressor starts. What should the evaluator measure first?
options: The voltage at the board and circuit during starting, with a logger
The brightness of each lamp, with a light meter, at midday on a sunny day
The insulation resistance of the lighting circuit cables
The earth rod resistance at the main earthing terminal

questions.stem: A thermal image shows one breaker terminal at 68 °C, while identical terminals carrying a similar current are at 41 °C. What is the most likely cause?
options: The breaker is new and is still running in
A loose or poor connection at that terminal
The camera is set to the wrong colour palette
The room is too cool for the breaker to work

questions.stem: Why is the temperature difference between similar parts (the 'delta T') used to rank hot spots in a board?
options: It shows the cost of the energy lost at each joint
It removes any need to know the load at that time
It compares like with like, so a real defect stands out
It tells the evaluator the exact age of each cable and joint

questions.stem: Why should the load current be recorded at the time a thermal survey is carried out?
options: The camera only works properly above a set level of load current
The client is billed by the load at that time
The load decides the colours shown in the image
Heat depends on current, so a light load can hide faults

questions.stem: A sub-main's insulation resistance was 200 MΩ, then 90 MΩ, then 15 MΩ at yearly tests. All are above the minimum. What should the evaluator conclude?
options: The steady fall is a warning sign, so find the cause
All the readings pass, so nothing needs to be done
The tester must be faulty, since the readings change
The cable is improving, because the numbers are lower

questions.stem: An installation from the 1970s has rubber-insulated cables that crack and crumble when moved. What should the evaluation recommend?
options: Paint the cables to seal up the cracks in the rubber
Use the circuits as normal, but avoid touching them
Plan to rewire, starting at once where it is worst
Raise the breaker sizes to stop the nuisance tripping

questions.stem: An evaluation finds many defects. How should the recommendations be ordered in the report?
options: By the cost of each repair, with the cheapest one put first
By risk: danger to people first, then damage, then savings
By the floor they are on, starting from the top floor
In the order the evaluator happened to find them

questions.stem: A risk matrix scores risk as likelihood × severity, each from 1 to 5. A defect is rated likelihood 4 and severity 5. What is its score?
The specification asked for armoured cable to a pump house, but PVC cable in plastic conduit was fitted. What should the evaluator do?
options: Record that it does not meet the specification and refer it
Accept it, because it works on the day of the visit
Rip it out at once without telling the contractor
Change the specification so that it matches the work that was done

questions.stem: A hotel's corridors have old 58 W fluorescent fittings lit 24 hours a day. Which option is best to evaluate?
options: Taking out every second fitting with no study
Fitting brighter lamps of the same old type in each fitting
LED fittings, with the savings and payback worked out
Switching the corridors off at night for the guests

questions.stem: New corridor fittings cost J$900 000 and save J$360 000 a year in energy. What is the simple payback period?
options: 0.4 years
2.5 years
3.6 years
5.4 years

questions.stem: An old fitting draws 70 W including its ballast. An LED replacement draws 24 W. How much energy does one fitting save in 24 hours?
options: 0.5 kWh
1.7 kWh
2.2 kWh
1.1 kWh

questions.stem: A building used 21 600 kWh in 30 days, and its maximum demand was 60 kW. What is its load factor (average demand ÷ maximum demand)?
A factory's power bill shows a charge for low power factor. What should the evaluation look into?
options: Swapping all the LED lamps for filament lamps
Raising the voltage at the main switchboard
Power factor correction, after measuring the load
Changing the frequency of the factory's supply to suit the motors

questions.stem: A school wants to run a new computer lab from an existing sub-board. What should be evaluated first?
options: The colour of the sub-board door and its lock
The sub-main rating, its logged demand and spare ways
The number of pupils who will use the lab each day
The make and model of the computers that the school has chosen

questions.stem: After a flood in Old Harbour, water stood 300 mm deep in a shop. What should the evaluation say about outlets and boards that were under water?
options: They may be switched back on as soon as they look dry inside
They can be dried with a hair dryer and used again
Only the outlets above the waterline need checking
Replace them, or check them as the maker says, before use

questions.stem: After a hurricane, the roof-mounted PV array at a school is broken. What must the evaluation make clear first?
options: The modules still make voltage in daylight, so are a shock risk
The panels will work again as soon as they have been washed down
The whole array can be reset from the inverter's screen
The damage only spoils how the roof looks from the road

questions.stem: Why does the evaluator talk to the building's maintenance staff?
options: To ask them to carry out the whole evaluation instead
To find out who is to blame for past faults
They know of trips, faults and changes not on record
To sell them a new maintenance contract

questions.stem: In a 200-room hotel, the evaluator checks 20 rooms in detail. What makes this sample useful?
options: Choosing the 20 rooms nearest the lift, to save time on site
Rooms from each floor and type, widened if faults are found
Checking only the rooms that the manager suggests
Checking only the newest rooms in the hotel

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports a finding in an evaluation report?
options: The evaluator's memory of what was seen
A guess based on the building's age
What a tenant said on the telephone
A dated photo, its location and the reading

questions.stem: An evaluation finds an overloaded, ageing sub-board. Which approach gives the client the best basis for a decision?
options: Options with costs, benefits, risks and a recommendation
One option only, so that the client is not confused
The most costly option, just to be on the safe side
No option, leaving the choice for the next evaluator

questions.stem: One replacement board is cheaper to buy but has a short life and no spares. Why compare the life-cycle cost of the boards?
options: The cheapest board to buy is always the best choice
The most costly board always lasts the longest
It counts buying, running, upkeep and replacing over time
It is needed only when the client is a government body or agency

questions.stem: Why should each finding in an evaluation report give its exact location (board, circuit and room)?
options: So the report looks longer and more complete
So the repair team can find and fix the right item
So the client can work out the evaluator's fee for each item
So the photos do not need any captions

questions.stem: During an evaluation, you find exposed live busbars in a board in a school corridor. What should you do?
options: Note it for the final report in two weeks' time
Take a photo of it and then carry on with the survey as planned
Tell the pupils to keep away from that corridor
Have it made safe and tell the client at once, in writing

questions.stem: A 110 V circuit measures 101 V at its far end on full load. What is the volt drop as a percentage of 110 V?
The design gave a sub-board a maximum demand of 40 A. A week's log now shows peaks of 58 A. What does this suggest?
options: The logger is wrong, because a design is always right
The design figure was set far too high at the start
Loads have grown, so check the cable and device ratings
The sub-board is now running at a lower voltage

questions.stem: A farm's earth electrode read 12 Ω when new and now reads 85 Ω. The design value is 20 Ω. What should the evaluator recommend?
options: Nothing, since the earth is still connected
Find the cause, such as a corroded rod or joint, and fix it
Remove the rod, since it is clearly no longer doing its job
Fit a larger main breaker to make up for the earth

questions.stem: A hotel's records show its transfer switch failed to change over to the generator twice last year. What should the evaluation report say?
options: The system is fine, because the generator did start
The transfer switch should be taken out to avoid any more trouble
The guests should be told to keep a torch in each room
Find and fix the cause, then prove it with a witnessed test

questions.stem: You lead a team evaluating a factory. A member finds a fault but says there is no time to record it. What should you insist on?
options: Each finding is recorded with its location and evidence first
Findings are remembered and written up the following week
Only the largest faults are written down on the day
Findings are passed on by word of mouth at the end

questions.stem: Before a board cover is removed so that load readings can be taken with a clamp meter, what must the evaluator have?
options: A ladder that is taller than the board
Permission from any staff member who is nearby
Authorisation, a risk assessment, PPE and a CAT-rated meter
A second meter, in case the first one breaks

questions.stem: Why should an evaluator check that a board's circuit chart matches the circuits it feeds?
options: So the painter knows which board to paint first
So people isolate the right circuit when they work on it
So the meter reader can find the main switch
So the board looks neat and tidy for all the client's visitors

questions.stem: During an evaluation of a warehouse, the main board is found blocked by stacked pallets. How should this be reported?
options: As a small point about tidiness only, with no action needed
As a matter for the warehouse staff and not the client
As a reason to move the board outside the building
As a safety issue, since it must be reached in an emergency

questions.stem: A server room trips off twice a month. The records show it began when more servers were added to one RCD-protected circuit. What is the likely cause?
options: The servers' normal earth leakage adds up on the one RCD
The servers draw much more current on Monday mornings than other days
The RCD is too large a rating for such a small room
The room's lights are on the same breaker as the A/C

questions.stem: Which recommendation in an evaluation report is the most useful?
options: 'Improve the electrical system soon.'
'Some of the boards are not very good.'
'Replace the 30-year-old kitchen sub-board within three months.'
'Look at the wiring when there is some time.'

questions.stem: Which is NOT a reason to evaluate an existing installation?
options: A change of use, such as a house becoming a shop
The installer wants to change his business name
Planned extra load, such as new A/C units
Damage after a fire, a flood or a hurricane

questions.stem: An evaluation estimates 40 hours of labour at J$2 500 an hour and J$150 000 of materials. What is the total before GCT?
Six months after an energy evaluation, the client asks whether the changes worked. What is the best way to show this?
options: Send the same report again with a new date on it
Ask the staff whether things feel any better than before
Measure again and compare with the first readings
Point out that nobody has complained since

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What instrument is left at a board to record voltage, current and power over days or weeks?
What is the set of measurements taken before any change is made, so that savings can be compared later, called?
An evaluation shows a 1.5 kW pump could run 2 hours a day less. How many kWh would that save in a 30-day month?
What is the short opening section of a report called, which gives the main findings and recommendations in a few lines?
What term describes the difference between a supply's rating and its peak demand: the room left for more load?
On some commercial power bills, what is the highest average demand in kW over a short set period, such as 15 minutes, called?
A logger records the voltage every 10 minutes for 7 days. How many readings does it make?
A shop's bill shows 9 000 kWh used in a 30-day month. What was its average demand, in kW?
Which document, sent by the power company each month, gives the energy used and is studied in an energy evaluation? (one or two words)
What are the unwanted currents at whole multiples of the 50 Hz supply frequency, caused by electronic loads, called?
A sub-board had a logged peak of 50 A. A new load of 18 A, used at the same time, is planned. What would the new peak be, in amps?
What is the usual unit for reactive power on a power analyser's display? (letters)
What is a short fall in supply voltage, such as when a large motor starts, called? (one word)
What is the expected number of years an item such as a board or a cable will last in use called? (two words)
In a thermal survey, what is the camera setting called that allows for how well a surface gives off heat?

essays.stem: An old hotel in Ocho Rios is to be refurbished. Describe how you would plan and carry out an evaluation of its electrical installation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would meet the owner to agree the purpose and scope in writing: which buildings and systems, what questions to answer (condition, capacity for the new layout, safety and energy use), the access I will have, and when shutdowns are possible. I would ask for drawings, test records, maintenance logs and a year of power bills. Next I would plan the team, the instruments with calibration in date, the risk assessment and the permits needed. On site I would inspect the boards, wiring and equipment, sampling rooms on each floor and widening the sample if faults appear. I would leave a power logger on the main board for at least a week, and do a thermal survey on load. Dead tests would be done on isolated circuits by a competent person. I would talk to the maintenance staff about trips and faults. Each finding is recorded with a photo, location and reading. Finally I would analyse the results, rank the risks and write a report with options and costs.
markingPoints: Agrees purpose, scope and access with the client in writing
Collects drawings, test records, logs and bills
Plans team, calibrated instruments, risk assessment and permits
Uses inspection, sampling, logging, thermal survey and safe dead testing, and interviews staff
Records evidence and reports ranked findings with options and costs

essays.stem: A restaurant wants to add a new kitchen line drawing 36 A. Its main switch is rated 100 A and a week's log shows a peak of 72 A. Explain how you would evaluate whether the installation can take the new load, and what you would recommend.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the logged figure is sound: a full week, including the busiest days, with the logger calibrated. Adding the new load to the peak gives 72 + 36 = 108 A, which is more than the 100 A main switch, so as it stands the installation cannot take it. I would also check the main cable's rating, the service from the power company, the board's spare ways and its busbar rating, and the earthing. I would look at whether the new line would really run at the busiest time, and share the loads across both lines. Options would be: an upgrade of the service, main switch, main cable and board, with the power company's agreement; moving some existing load, such as water heating, to off-peak times; or load management so certain items cannot run together. I would recommend the upgrade if growth is likely, give costs for each option, and say the new line must not be connected until the chosen work is done.
markingPoints: Checks the logged data is valid
Works out 72 + 36 = 108 A, over the 100 A rating
Checks cable, service, board, busbars and earthing
Gives options: upgrade, moving load, load management
Makes a recommendation with costs and says not to connect until done

essays.stem: Explain how a thermal imaging survey is used in evaluating an installation. Say how you make the results trustworthy and how you rank what you find.
essays.modelAnswer: A thermal camera shows the surface temperatures of boards, joints and cables, so poor connections, overloaded parts and unbalanced loads show up as hot spots without switching anything off. To make the results trustworthy, the survey is done when the building is on normal or heavy load, after it has been running for some hours, and the load current on each circuit is recorded, because heat depends on current. The camera's emissivity is set for the surface, because shiny metal reflects heat and can give false readings. Covers are removed only by an authorised person with a risk assessment and suitable PPE, or viewing windows are used. Each hot spot is photographed with a normal photo for location. To rank them, I compare each part with a similar part on the same load (the delta T) and with the air temperature, and use the client's or the specification's priority bands. The largest differences are reported for urgent repair, and every repair is checked with a second survey.
markingPoints: Explains what thermal imaging shows and why it is useful
Surveys on load and records the load current
Sets emissivity correctly and pairs images with normal photos
Safe access: authorised person, risk assessment, PPE or viewing windows
Ranks by delta T against priority bands, and rechecks after repair

essays.stem: An office has 120 old fittings drawing 70 W each, lit 10 hours a day on 260 days a year. LED fittings of 24 W would cost J$1 800 000 to fit, and the assessor's tariff is J$60 per kWh. Work out the yearly saving and the simple payback, and explain what else the evaluation should consider.
essays.modelAnswer: Each fitting saves 70 − 24 = 46 W. For 120 fittings, that is 46 × 120 = 5 520 W, or 5.52 kW. The fittings run 10 × 260 = 2 600 hours a year, so the energy saved is 5.52 × 2 600 = 14 352 kWh a year. At J$60 per kWh, the saving is 14 352 × 60 = J$861 120 a year. The simple payback is 1 800 000 ÷ 861 120 = about 2.1 years. The evaluation should also check that the new fittings give the light levels the rooms need, since fewer or dimmer fittings may not be acceptable. It should consider adding occupancy and daylight sensors for more savings, the longer life and lower upkeep of LEDs, and the lower heat, which reduces the A/C load. It should note how the old fittings will be disposed of safely, and recommend measuring a baseline first so the real saving can be checked afterwards.
markingPoints: Works out 5.52 kW saved
Works out 2 600 hours and 14 352 kWh a year
Works out J$861 120 a year saving
Works out a simple payback of about 2.1 years
Considers light levels, controls, upkeep, A/C, disposal or a baseline

essays.stem: Explain how you would rank the defects found in an evaluation and present them to the client. Use a risk score (likelihood × severity) and give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: I would score each defect for likelihood, how likely it is to cause harm, and severity, how bad the harm would be, each on a scale of 1 to 5. Multiplying them gives a risk score up to 25. For example, exposed live parts in a board that staff open often might be likelihood 4 and severity 5, a score of 20: this is urgent and must be made safe at once and reported in writing that day. A missing RCD on outlets by a kitchen sink might score 3 × 5 = 15, needing action within weeks. Overheated but sound joints might score 3 × 3 = 9, for planned repair. Missing circuit labels might score 2 × 2 = 4, a lower priority but still worth doing. I would present the findings in a table, highest score first, each with its location, photo, the action needed, a suggested time to act and a rough cost. This helps the client spend money where it matters most for safety.
markingPoints: Explains likelihood and severity scales and multiplying them
Gives a high-risk example with immediate action
Gives medium and low examples with suitable timescales
Presents a ranked table with location, evidence, action, time and cost
Explains that ranking directs money to the greatest risks

essays.stem: A contractor says a new office installation is complete. Explain how you would evaluate it against the specification before the client accepts it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would gather the contract, the specification, the design drawings and schedules, and the contractor's test records and certificates. I would draw up a checklist from the specification: materials, cable types and sizes, containment, devices, labels, earthing and bonding, and the tests required. On site I would check the work against the checklist, sampling enough circuits and rooms on each floor, and widen the sample if I find faults. I would check that the test results are complete, signed, within the limits, and taken with calibrated instruments, and witness some retests if needed. Any item that does not meet the specification goes on a non-conformance list with its location and evidence. Small items go on a snag list with dates for completion. I would report to the client whether the installation can be accepted, accepted with listed snags, or not accepted until defects are put right, and confirm that the as-built drawings and manuals are supplied.
markingPoints: Gathers contract, specification, drawings and test records
Builds a checklist from the specification
Checks on site with a fair sample, widening it if faults are found
Checks test results are complete, valid and within limits; witnesses retests
Lists non-conformances and snags, and reports a clear accept or reject decision

essays.stem: Describe how you would evaluate a small business's installation after a hurricane has brought down trees and flooded the ground floor, before any power is restored.
essays.modelAnswer: Safety comes first. I would make sure the supply is off and locked off at the main switch, confirm with the power company that its service is isolated if the service cable is damaged, and prove dead with a tester checked before and after use. I would check that any generator cannot start and that its changeover switch is safe, so nothing back-feeds. A PV array still makes voltage in daylight, so I would treat it as live and keep away from damaged panels and cables until the DC side is made safe by a trained person. Then I would walk the site and record damage: the service mast, meter, outdoor units, cables under fallen trees. I would note how high the water rose. Boards, outlets, breakers and RCDs that were under water would normally be replaced, or checked as the makers say. Cables are dried and insulation tested by a competent person. My report lists what must be replaced or repaired and in what order before re-energising.
markingPoints: Isolates, locks off and proves dead, involving the power company if needed
Prevents generator back-feed and treats PV as live
Surveys and records the damage, including flood height
Replaces or checks flooded equipment as the makers say, and tests cables
Reports the repairs needed and their order before re-energising

essays.stem: An evaluation finds that a 35-year-old office installation is worn, overloaded and poorly recorded. Compare repairing it, upgrading parts of it and replacing it completely, and explain how you would help the client choose.
essays.modelAnswer: Repairing means fixing the defects found, such as loose joints and damaged accessories, and adding labels. It costs least and causes little disruption, but it does not solve the overload or the age of the wiring, so faults will keep coming. Upgrading parts means replacing the worst items, such as the main board and the most overloaded sub-mains, and adding circuits and RCDs. It costs more, but fixes the main risks and adds capacity, though old wiring remains. Replacing everything costs the most and needs the building empty or worked in stages, but gives a modern, safe, recorded installation with capacity for the future and a long life. To help the client choose, I would set out each option's cost, the risk left behind, the disruption, and the life-cycle cost over, say, 15 years, including repairs and energy. I would recommend one option with clear reasons, and a plan for staging the work.
markingPoints: Repair: lowest cost, little disruption, but problems remain
Partial upgrade: fixes main risks and adds capacity, old wiring remains
Full replacement: highest cost and disruption, safest and longest life
Compares cost, risk, disruption and life-cycle cost
Makes a reasoned recommendation with staging

essays.stem: Explain how you would use a power logger to find and evaluate power quality problems in a busy office: voltage drops, unbalanced lines, harmonics and poor power factor.
essays.modelAnswer: With authorisation and a risk assessment, the logger is connected at the main board by a competent person, using a CAT-rated instrument and PPE, and left for at least a week. It records the voltage, current on each line and the neutral, power, power factor and harmonics. Afterwards I would compare the voltages with the specification's limits, and look for dips at the times large loads start or the busiest hours, which may point to long or small cables or loose joints. I would compare the line currents to see if the lines are unbalanced, which raises the neutral current, and plan to move circuits. High harmonics and a neutral current larger than expected point to many electronic loads, and may need a larger neutral or filters. A low power factor points to motor loads, and power factor correction can be considered. I would present the graphs, the causes found and the actions recommended.
markingPoints: Connects the logger safely, with authorisation, CAT-rated meter and PPE, for about a week
Compares voltages with limits and looks for dips and their causes
Checks line balance and neutral current, and plans rebalancing
Identifies harmonics and suitable actions
Identifies poor power factor and correction, and presents findings

essays.stem: Describe the structure and contents of a good evaluation report for a client, and explain how you would present it.
essays.modelAnswer: The report starts with a title page giving the site, the client, the date and the evaluator. A short summary follows, with the overall finding and the most urgent recommendations, for a busy reader. Next comes the scope: what was evaluated, what was not, and why. The method section says how the work was done: inspection, sampling, logging, thermal survey and tests, with the instruments and their calibration. The findings are set out by area or system, each with its location, evidence such as photos and readings, and the risk score. The recommendations are ranked, with timescales and rough costs, and options where there is a choice. Appendices hold the logger graphs, test schedules and thermal images. I would send the report ahead of a meeting, then go through it with the client, starting with any danger, answer questions in plain words, and agree the next steps in writing.
markingPoints: Title page and short summary
Scope and method, with instruments
Findings with location, evidence and risk
Ranked recommendations with timescales, costs and options; appendices
Presents in a meeting, danger first, and agrees next steps

practical1.title: Evaluate a training installation against its specification
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a training installation that is NOT connected to any supply (a board feeding lighting, outlet and fixed-appliance circuits), with its specification, a design drawing and a set of past records. The assessor has planted defects and departures from the specification, such as a wrong cable size, a missing RCD, a wrong label, a loose terminal and a missing record. As a group, give each member a role (lead evaluator, two inspectors, records reviewer, and report writer) and swap so everyone inspects. Isolate and lock off the supply point with every member's padlock and a tag, and prove dead with a tester checked before and after use. Make a checklist from the specification. Inspect the installation and check the records against what is installed. Carry out dead tests (continuity and insulation resistance) on two circuits and compare them with the past records. The assessor then hands out a thermal image and a week of logged load data for the same board; add these to the evidence. Record each finding on a findings register with its location, photo, evidence and a risk score.
materials: Training installation with planted defects, not connected to any supply
Specification, design drawing and past records (from the assessor)
Lock-off kit with a multi-lock hasp, one padlock per member, and tags
Two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Thermal image and logged load data sheets (from the assessor)
Blank checklist and findings register forms
photos: The checklist made from the specification
The supply point locked off with every member's padlock and a tag
The tester checked on the proving unit before and after proving dead
Each defect found, with a label showing the finding number
The dead test results set beside the past records
The completed findings register with risk scores
checklist: Helped build a checklist from the specification
Isolated, locked off and proved dead correctly, with the tester checked before and after
Found and recorded defects and departures from the specification
Carried out a dead test correctly and compared it with past records
Used the thermal image and logged data correctly as evidence
Gave sensible risk scores and recorded the location and evidence of each finding
Left the installation, tools and papers safe and tidy
safety: The installation stays dead and locked off throughout; only the instructor energises anything
Every member fits their own padlock before any cover is opened
Warn others before each insulation test and let the circuit discharge before touching it
Report any real (not planted) danger to the assessor at once

practical2.title: Evaluate a building's data and present an upgrade report
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group an evaluation pack for a made-up two-storey office in Montego Bay: a single-line diagram, the board schedules, a week of logged data for the main board (voltages, line currents, neutral current, power factor), twelve months of power bills, thermal images of three boards with load currents, insulation test results from three past years, and a list of planned new loads. As a group, give each member a role (lead evaluator, capacity analyst, energy analyst, condition analyst, and report editor) and swap so that each member checks another's sums. Work out the spare capacity and whether the new loads fit, the line balance and neutral current, the load factor from the bills, and the ranking of the thermal hot spots. Look for trends in the insulation results. Work out the energy saving and simple payback of one improvement, using the assessor's prices. Write a short evaluation report with a summary, ranked findings and costed options. Present it to the assessor, who plays the client, and answer questions.
materials: Evaluation pack for a made-up office (from the assessor)
Calculators, rulers, highlighters and A3 paper
Blank report template and findings register
Flip chart or whiteboard for the presentation
photos: The capacity and line balance working
The load factor and energy saving sums
The thermal hot spots ranked with their delta T
The written report with its summary and ranked findings
The presentation to the client, with the flip chart
checklist: Worked out spare capacity and the effect of new loads correctly
Worked out line balance and neutral current correctly
Ranked the thermal hot spots sensibly using delta T and load
Spotted the trend in the insulation results
Worked out an energy saving and payback correctly
Wrote part of the report clearly with evidence
Presented findings clearly and answered the client's questions
safety: This is a desk and presentation task: no equipment is opened or energised
Any finding of danger must be shown first in the report and the presentation
Treat the made-up client's information as confidential, as you would on a real job
